page_checks.summary: Factitive themes come into existence through an event; path, source, goal, location, recipient and beneficiary are distinct semantic roles.
Canonical one-agent/one-patient clauses align the agent with subject and patient with direct object, but psychological and causer roles have distinct alignments.
Subject function has agency/topic-like prototypes, but its identity is syntactic; semantic perspective can determine selection across psychological predicates.
Canonical finite clauses have subjects, including NPs or sometimes subordinate clauses; imperative and nonfinite subject omissions are licensed.
Subject–predicator position, nominative/accusative case, agreement and auxiliary inversion distinguish subject from object in canonical finite clauses.
Subject open interrogatives retain ordinary order; nonsubject wh interrogatives often invert the auxiliary, tags track the subject, and VP coordination tests identify it.
Maximal finite reduction preserves subject under ordinary ellipsis; a coordinated NP occupies one subject function; the passive/preposing diagnostic table begins.
Position, case, agreement, inversion, interrogative form, tag, coordination and obligatoriness in table show passive promotes a new subject while preposing preserves the old one.
Passive by-phrases internalize an active subject as a non-core complement; extraposition and existential constructions use dummy it/there as syntactic subjects.
Extraposition shows agreement with it, whereas existentials ordinarily match a displaced NP; informal contracted there's may appear with plural NPs.
Interrogatives, tags, coordination and reduction confirm dummy subjects; subject–auxiliary inversion differs structurally from subject postposing.
Postauxiliary and clause-final subject positions differ; a fronted adjunct or predicative can license a postposed subject, whereas an ordinary object cannot.
The direct object is a core complement in mono- and ditransitive clauses; a PP with its own NP complement is not a direct object of the verb.
Objecthood involves core status, lexical licensing and passive correspondence, but the passive test is sufficient rather than necessary.
Direct objects normally follow predicators, with particle, heavy-object and fronting exceptions; in object extraposition dummy it is object, not the following clause.
The ditransitive construction contains Oi then Od, whereas its to/for alternant contains one Od and a PP complement; some two-pronoun orders are dialectal.
Indirect-object passives are generally preferred, while direct-object ditransitive passives have verb-specific, regional and register-sensitive limits.
The indirect object resists postposing, fronting and certain predicand/gap-control patterns that a direct object can sometimes support.
Canonical clauses with a single object have a direct object even if its semantic role is recipient-like; predicative complements are distinguished from objects.
Predicative complements are usually AdjPs or nonreferential NPs and provide a property of their predicand; semantic arguments need not coincide with syntactic complements.
